truculent.e: First attested circa 1540, from Middle French, from Latin truculentus (“fierce, savage”), from trux (“fierce, wild”).
truculent.x: The truculent soldiers gave us a steely-eyed stare.

trudge.e: Mid-16th century. Original meaning was somewhat idiomatic, meaning "to walk using snowshoes." Probably of Scandinavian origin, compare Icelandic þrúga (“snowshoe”)…
trudge.x: The morning after the landslip, with rain still pouring down, it was an unpleasant trudge through deep mud to get there.

truffle.e: Borrowed from French trufle, a variant of truffe (whence also Danish and Norwegian trøffel, Swedish tryffel, German Trüffel), from Old Occitan trufa, a metathesis of Late…
truffle.x: In ancient times, the Romans imported truffles, credited with marked aphrodisiac virtue, from Libya as well as Greece.

truism.x: The phrase If something exists, there is porn of it used to be a clever internet meme; now it’s a truism.

trump.e: Possibly from French triomphe (“triumph”) or Old French triumphe. If so, it is a doublet of triumph and thriambus. Compare German Trumpf.
trump.x: And now her Heart with Pleasure jumps, She scarce remembers what is Trumps.

trumpet.e: From Middle English trumpet, trumpette, trompette (“trumpet”), from Old French trompette (“trumpet”), diminutive of trompe (“horn, trump, trumpet”), from Frankish…
trumpet.x: The royal herald sounded a trumpet to announce their arrival.

trumpeter.e: From trumpet + -er (occupational suffix) or + -er (agent noun suffix).
trumpeter.x: Booster is not a loud trumpeter as elephants go.

truncheon.e: From Middle English tronchoun, from Old French tronchon (“thick stick”), from Late Latin *troncionem, from Latin truncus.

truss.e: From Middle English trusse, from Old French trousse, torse, from Vulgar Latin *torsus, variant of Classical Latin tortus, past participle of torqueō.
truss.x: A truss may keep the abdominal contents from protruding into the hernial sac; however, this won't cure the hernia.

trustworthy.x: The storage of cryptographic secrets is one of the paramount requirements in building trustworthy systems.

truthful.e: From truth + -ful. Piecewise doublet of trothful, from Middle English trouþeful.
truthful.x: Mr. Musk was not being truthful, Mr. Rubio said. What about the more than 1,500 State Department officials who took early retirement in buyouts?

tryst.e: From Middle English tryst, trist, from Old French triste, tristre (“waiting place, appointed station in hunting”), probably from a North Germanic source such as Old Norse…
tryst.x: A silence supreme and altogether European. Shutters drawn, shops barred. A red glow here and there to mark a tryst.

tsarist.e: From tsar + -ist. Piecewise doublet of Caesarist.

tsetse.x: Species of Trypanosoma transmitted by tsetse cause diseases of economic importance in humans and domestic animals in sub-Saharan Africa.

tsunami.e: Borrowed from Japanese 津波 (tsunami), from 津 (tsu, “harbour”) + 波 (nami, “wave”).
tsunami.x: A wave simulator in the tank can re-enact tsunamis and northeasters, and imitate wave conditions from midocean.

tsundere.e: Borrowed from Japanese ツンデレ (tsundere), from つんつん (tsun-tsun, “in a cross, aloof, or standoffish manner”, adverb) + でれでれ (dere-dere, “in a lovey-dovey, infatuated, or…

tubercle.e: Derived from Latin tūberculum. Compare tuber.

tugboat.e: From tug + boat. Sense 2 from monthly tugboat, a reference to the saying "our ship has come in," here referring to a small, "reliable" "tugboat" instead of a large…

tuition.e: From Anglo-Norman tuycioun, from Old French tuicion, from Latin tuitiō (“guard, protection, defense”), from tuēri (“to watch, guard, see, observe”).
tuition.x: Tuition in the past was like taking medicine and you sent children for it only if they were doing poorly in a subject.

tulip.e: From Middle French tulipe, from earlier tulipan, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (tülbent, dülbent, “cheesecloth”), from Classical Persian دلبند (dulband, “turban”).

tulle.e: Borrowed from French tulle, named after French Tulle (a town), named after Latin Tūtēla (a Roman deity), from Latin tūtēla (whence English tutelary), from Latin tueor…
tulle.x: ‘Before I forget, there is one turquoise tulle fabric I think you would love . . .’

tumble.x: He who tumbles from a tower surely has a greater blow than he who slides from a molehill.

tumbler.x: I poured out some whisky into a tumbler, and gave it to him.

tumbleweed.x: Putting an ad in the local paper that Spock's Beard and Arena are in town will get you a tumbleweed response and some wasted revenue.

tumor.e: From Middle English tumour, from Old French tumour, from Latin tumor (“swelling”), from tumeō (“bulge, swell”, verb), from Proto-Italic *tumēō, from Proto-Indo-European…

tumult.e: From Old French tumulte, from Latin tumultus (“noise, tumult”).
tumult.x: Till in loud tumult all the Greeks arose.

tumultuous.e: From Old French tumultuous (modern French tumultueux), from Latin tumultuōsus (“restless, turbulent”), from tumultus (“disturbance, uproar, violent commotion, tumult.
tumultuous.x: Down showers tumultuous music from the belfry of Old Trinity— / Merry chiming for His birth, and gave songs for His Divinity!

tundra.x: We parcel up time into years and months and days because without compartmentalisation the tundra of time is impossible to navigate.

tungsten.x: There was a bar of tungsten on the bench, and they were invited to feel how heavy it was.

tunic.e: Borrowed from Middle French tunique, from Latin tunica, possibly from Semitic (compare Aramaic [script needed] (kittuna), Hebrew כותנת (kuttoneth, “coat”), English…

turban.e: Borrowed from Middle French turbant, from Italian turbante, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (tülbent), from Classical Persian دلبند (dulband), also the root of tulip.
turban.x: ‘Nay, I cannot move another step,’ he howled. ‘I am old and my turban is lost. Arré! Arré!’

turbid.x: On the 6th October, the 18th day of her illness, she presented the following phenomena: — pulse small and quick — urine yellow and turbid.

turbine.e: Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbō, turbinem (“tornado, whirlwind; crowd”).

turbot.e: From Middle English turbot, turbut, from Anglo-Norman turbut, Old French turbot, torbot, from Old Swedish tornbut, from törn (“thorn”) + but (“butt, flatfish”).
turbot.x: “With vegetables in it, you know. Then turbot with thick sauce, then ... roast beef; and mind it’s good. Yes, and capons, perhaps, and then sweets.”

turbulence.e: From Middle English turbulence (“turbidity, cloudiness”), from Late Latin turbulentia (“trouble, disquiet”). By surface analysis, turbulent + -ence.

turbulent.e: From Middle English turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus, from turba (“disorder, tumult, crowd”).
turbulent.x: It is dangerous to sail in turbulent seas.

tureen.e: From earlier terrene (thus pronunciations with /tj/, /t͡ʃ/ are spelling pronunciations), borrowed from French terrine. Doublet of terrine.

turmeric.e: From Middle English turmeryte, tarmaret, of uncertain origin. Possibly corrupted from Arabic كُرْكُم (kurkum, “Curcuma”) or from Old French terre mérite (“deserving…

turmoil.e: Unknown. First appears c. 1526. Perhaps from Old French tremouille (“the hopper of a mill”).
turmoil.x: The Taoists developed their philosophy during an extended era of turmoil known as the Warring States period of Chinese history.

turncoat.e: A compound of turn + coat, reportedly derived from the sometime military practice of wearing uniform coats that were lined in material of a contrasting color, and which…

turnip.e: From Middle English turnepe, probably from turn + Middle English nepe, from Old English nǣp, from Latin nāpus.
turnip.x: In general, beets, carrots, and turnips are all of aphrodisiac value in erotic dietary.

turnkey.e: From turn + key. (jailer): Compare typologically Russian вертуха́й (vertuxáj) (akin to верте́ть (vertétʹ)).

turnout.x: Depending on the location of a restaurant, weekdays may equally experience low turnout.

turnpike.e: From Middle English turnpyke (“spiked barrier across a road”), originally used to block access to such a road until a toll was paid.

turnstile.x: The fare was fixed at 2d., irrespective of distance, and was paid by passengers on passing through turnstiles at each station.

turpentine.e: From Middle English terebentyne, terbentyne, turbentine, from Old French terbentine, turbentine, Latin terebinthina, from Ancient Greek τερεβινθίνη (terebinthínē), the…
turpentine.x: Turpentine timber was obtained from the forests outside Maryborough and Townsville, and shipped by rail and landing craft to Hayman Island.

turquoise.e: From Middle French turquoise, from Old French (pierre) turquoise (“Turkish (stone)”), from turc + -ois.

turret.e: From Middle English touret, from Old French torete (French tourette), diminutive of tour (“tower”), from Latin turris. Doublet of tor, tourelle, and tower. See tower.
turret.x: Their Victorian house had three turrets and a large amount of gingerbread trim.

tutor.e: From Middle English tutour, from Old French tuteur (French tuteur), from Latin tūtor (“a watcher, protector, guardian”), from tueor (“protect”); see tuition.
tutor.x: He passed the difficult class with help from his tutor.

tutorial.e: The adjective is from tutor (noun) + -ial, ultimately from Latin tūtor (“watcher, protector, defender”). The noun is transferred from the adjective.

tuxedo.e: From Tuxedo Park, New York, US, where the fashion is often said to have originated, the village in turn likely from an Eastern Algonquian language (Munsee), from Lenape…
tuxedo.x: He wore a tuxedo for his sister's wedding.

twaddle.e: An alteration of twattle (1556), of unknown origin.
twaddle.x: You're talking a load of twaddle. Get your facts straight, man!

tweak.e: From Middle English twikken, from Old English twiccian (“to pluck”), from Proto-West Germanic *twekkōn (“to fasten; clamp; pinch”). Related to twitch.
tweak.x: If we tweak the colors towards blue, it will look more natural.

tweed.e: Attested since the 1830s. Probably a shortening or back-formation from Scots tweedling (“a type of twilled cloth”), attested since the 16th century and related to…
tweed.x: “Nothing very special, sir. He had a mack or coat over his arm, and a trilby hat. He wore a tweed suit, sir, I think.”

tweet.e: Onomatopoeic of the sound made by a bird. Compare twitter. The social media senses evolved from earlier Twitter update, twit (noun), twitter (verb).
tweet.x: Every few seconds, a tweet appears and vanishes somewhere on the globe.

twelfth.e: From Middle English twelfthe, twelfte, from Old English twelfta (“twelfth”), from Proto-Germanic *twaliftô (“twelfth”), equivalent to twelve + -th (ordinal suffix).

twerk.e: Blend of twitch + jerk. The "sexually-provocative dance" sense was particularly popularized since c.
twerk.x: Note of male on territory, a loud kurr or twerk.

twilight.e: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English twilight, twyelyghte, equivalent to twi- (“double, half-”) + light, literally ‘second light, half-light’.
twilight.x: I could just make out her face in the twilight.

twirl.e: Of Scandinavian origin, akin to Norwegian Nynorsk tvirla, Old High German dweran (German zwirlen, quirlen), Dutch dwarrelen and Icelandic þyrill.
twirl.x: The conductor gave his baton a twirl, and the orchestra began to play.

twitter.e: From Middle English twitren, twiteren, from Old English *twiterian, from Proto-West Germanic *twitwiʀōn, from Proto-Germanic *twitwizōną (“to chirp; twitter”).
twitter.x: I often listen to the twitter of the birds in the park.

tycoon.e: Borrowed from Japanese 大君 (“great lord, prince”), a title for the shōgun. Related to taipan, from Cantonese 大班 (daai⁶ baan¹).
tycoon.x: Dagobert had only one customer, an American who wore square, rimless glasses and a beige suit and looked like a Wall Street tycoon.

typhoon.e: English texts mention typhon, tiphon as a Greek word for "whirlwind" since at least the 1550s, referring to Ancient Greek τυφῶν (tuphôn), τυφώς (tuphṓs, “whirlwind”) (the…

typhus.e: From New Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “fever, stupor”), from τύφω (túphō, “to smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-, extended form of *dʰew-…
typhus.x: Typhoid and typhus have similar names and symptoms, but are different diseases.

typography.e: From French typographie from Medieval Latin typographia from Ancient Greek τυπογράφος (tupográphos, “certified copy”) + -ίᾱ (-íā).

tyrannical.e: From Latin tyrannicus + -al; ultimately from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos) (absolute ruler, despot).

tyrannize.e: From Middle French tyranniser, equivalent to tyranny + -ize.
tyrannize.x: The prince tyrannized over his subjects.

tyranny.e: Inherited from Middle English tirannye, from Old French tyrannie, from Medieval Latin tyrannia, tyrania, from Ancient Greek τυραννία (turannía, “tyranny”), from τύραννος…
tyranny.x: Control, dispossession, violence, and tyranny are not “defensive”: they are part of an organized, ongoing aggression.

tyrant.e: From Middle English tyraunt, tiraunt, tyrant, tyrante, from Old French tyrant, from the addition of a terminal -t to tiran (cp.
tyrant.x: I am the Sonne of Marcus Cato, hoe. A Foe to Tyrants, and my Countries Friend.

tzatziki.e: From Greek τζατζίκι (tzatzíki), from Ottoman Turkish جاجیق (cacık). Doublet of cacik.
